Mechanically Modulated Reflect-Arrays for Vibration Monitoring of Aircraft Engines

Scroll through the working principle, unit cell design, and simulated response of a passive, wireless vibration sensor.

Scroll
Section 01

Background and Motivation

(a) Why monitor engine vibration?

With the era of technology and globalization, the demand for aviation for use in transportation, trade and other industries is at an all-time high. In 2022, aviation contributes around 2% of global CO₂ production alone, with reports showing that international aviation emissions are expected to triple by 2050 relative to 2015 if these levels are left unaddressed. Aviation also makes up 3.8–4% of total EU greenhouse gas emissions, and is the second-biggest source of GHG emissions within the transport sector, behind road transport.

Monitoring engine health is one of the key areas which can be improved to control the rate of emissions from these engines. Vibration monitoring and analysis is important to upholding engine maintenance. Engine maintenance directly affects combustion efficiency. Imbalance in rotating components, bearing wear, and blade degradation all increase fuel burn and pollutant output well before they become safety-critical faults. Vibration is one of the earliest and most information-rich signs of this kind of mechanical distress, making continuous monitoring a route to predictive maintenance: catching a fault while it's still cheap, safe, and fuel-efficient to fix, rather than after it has already degraded engine performance.

Section 01

(b) Why metamaterials for monitoring engine vibration?

According to the UK Metamaterials Network (UKMMN), a metamaterial is defined as: 'a 3D structure with a response or function due to the collective effect of meta-atom elements that is not possible to achieve conventionally with any individual constituent material'. A metasurface is a 2D version of a metamaterial , a thin, engineered surface built from sub-wavelength unit cells that collectively control the amplitude, phase, or polarisation of an incident wave, exactly the mechanism this sensor relies on.

Conventional vibration-monitoring systems may require powered sensors, signal-conditioning electronics and wiring. Temperature, vibration and cable routing can make installation and maintenance challenging in some engine locations. A passive microwave scatterer could reduce the components needed at the sensing location. The proof of concept metasurface's potential advantages include:

  • No onboard battery: the sensing tag is powered by the externally supplied microwave signal.
  • No tag wiring: the proposed sensing location would be interrogated wirelessly.
  • Fewer onboard components: the tag has no active sensing electronics.
  • Thermal suitability to test: durability under engine-relevant conditions remains to be established.
  • Weight-saving : a complete system comparison has not yet been made.
  • Maintenance : service-life benefits require long-term testing.

This motivates a fundamentally different sensing paradigm: rather than relying on active electronics to detect and transmit a vibration signal, a mechanically modulated metasurface encodes vibration directly into the phase of a backscattered microwave signal. Flexing the metasurface under vibration modulates its own electromagnetic response; no battery, no onboard power, and no electronic components are required at all.

Section 02

Unit Cell of Metasurface Array: Design and Principles

(i) Element dimensions

The unit cell design is referenced from Ball, R.F.; Ford, K.L.; Henthorn, S.D. "Mechanical Tuning of a Passive Battery-Less Huygens’ Scatterer for Small Insect Pollinator Tracking." Eng. Proc. 2026, 127, 26. The dimensions in the tables were scaled from the cited geometry to target a resonance near the 2.4 GHz ISM band. The multilayer stack is this project’s adaptation, rather than the structure reported by Ball et al. The sensing element builds on the electromagnetic characteristics of the electrically small Huygens-source geometry developed by Ziolkowski and Ball: an Egyptian Axe Dipole (EAD) near-field resonant parasitic element providing an electric-dipole response, paired with a capacitively loaded loop (CLL) element providing a complementary magnetic-dipole response. The scattered field of a Huygens-type element is the superposition of these two contributions, and the resulting directional response depends on their relative amplitude and phase, the central physical principle behind Huygens sources and Huygens metasurfaces.

These Huygen's scatterers which function as an electrically small antenna are compiled into a multilayered cascaded stack with Polyimide interlayers in between the Huygen layers. The EAD and CLL elements are not identical across all five layers: the arm lengths, labelled E₁, E₂, E₃ for the magnetic loop and e₁, e₂,₃ for the electric element, are the arm lengths in layers 1, 2, and 3 of the five-layer stack respectively, and vary between layer 1 and layers 2–3, while every other dimension stays fixed. Each cell is patterned on a 25 μm polyimide substrate (εr = 3.5, tan δ ≈ 0.003) with 50 μm polyimide interlayers.

doi.org/10.3390/engproc2026127026

Section 02

(ii) Geometry and design basis

As seen in the animation , the five layer cascaded stack of the unit cell is layered with the EAD and CLL elements in each layer. The EAD and CLL elements are not identical across all five layers: the arm lengths, labelled E₁, E₂, E₃ for the magnetic loop and e₁, e₂, e₃ for the electric element, are the arm lengths in layers 1, 2, and 3 of the five-layer stack respectively, and vary between layer 1 and layers 2–3, while every other dimension stays fixed. Each cell is patterned on a 25 μm polyimide substrate (εr = 3.5, tan δ ≈ 0.003) with 50 μm polyimide interlayers.

Rotational symmetry was retained, reducing the design's sensitivity to the orientation of the incident linear polarisation. This Huygens geometry is treated as the established starting architecture, not as a balance that automatically survives the multilayer modifications that follow: the electric and magnetic responses must be re-tuned once combined, and changing their geometry can shift which response dominates.

Section 02

(iii) Array formation

Each unit cell is translated to produce a 3x3 metasurface array as shown in the animation. The Huygens-scatterer geometry and dimensions of Ball et al. were replicated, then scaled by a factor of 1.7 to shift the unit cell's resonance to 2.4 GHz. Once the unit cells were cascaded into the five-layer stack, the full array was rescaled by a further factor of 0.8 to restore a 2.4 GHz resonance at the array level, since stacking shifts the response of the individual layers

Section 02

(iv) Directivity simulations of the unit cell and array

The simulated far-field directivity from CST, at the frequency of highest RCS, is consistent with predominantly electric-dipolar radiation, matching the standard angular dependence of a conventional electric dipole, U(θ) ∝ sin²(θ), where θ is measured from the dipole axis: radiation is minimum along the axis and maximum perpendicular to it, producing a toroidal three-dimensional pattern.

Section 03

Working Principle: Mechanical Modulation

(a) Sensor placement

The proof of principle metasurface sensor is proposed to mount on the engine's outer casing, near the inlet cowl lip, where it can sense vibration transmitted through the casing structure without needing access to the engine's high temperature interior. Vibration transmitted through that structure might bend the tag and change its microwave backscatter. This location and its mechanical and thermal suitability have not yet been validated on an engine. The proposed tag would need no local battery or wired signal connection, although an external RF reader would still be required.

Section 03

(b) Flexural bending

Flexural bending of the metasurface modulates the coupling between the EAD electric element and the CLL magnetic element within each unit cell. As the array conforms to a cylindrical bend, the coupling between the electric and magnetic elements gives rise to a phase shift in the backscattered signal, which is then detected and analyzed to determine the vibration frequency and amplitude. Here, CST simulations of the unit cell and array are modelled to sweep from a flat 0° up to 60° with 10° increments, as proof of concept to capture the full range of bending angles expected in the engine environment.

Because the array is entirely passive, no battery or onboard electronics are required: the mechanical deformation acts as stimulus for the phase modulation of the sensor.

Section 04

Experimental Setup

(a) Fabrication and assembly of unit cell and array

Each metal layer was fabricated externally (JLCPCB, Guangdong), then hand-stacked with Kapton interlayers and bonded with a thin layer of ethyl 2-cyanoacrylate (εr = 5.2, tan δ = 0.04) as adhesive, a process that introduced slight misalignment between layers.

RCS and phase were measured under an NRL arch, with two horn antennas positioned 5° from normal, calibrated against a 31.60 mm steel reference sphere. Each measurement was repeated three times, with the sample repositioned between runs, to confirm repeatability.

As discussed in Section 03(b), the experiment aimed to replicate the flexural bending of both unit cell and array as simulated in CST. The assembled metasurface array and unit cell stack were then mounted on 3D-printed PLA rigs (εr = 2.54, tan δ = 0.0071), designed in Fusion 360, one per bending angle from 0° to 60° in 10° steps, matching the CST sweep.

Section 05

Unit Cell: RCS & Phase

CST predicts a unit cell resonance of −22.7 dBsm at 2.32 GHz, with a phase span of about 2.02 rad at that peak. The fabricated unit cell instead resonates at −29.6 dBsm near 4.94 GHz, where the phase span is only around 2 rad.

The largest phase span, up to 6 rad, however, occurs off-resonance at 5.48 GHz, in an RCS trough, a shift attributed to layer misalignment during hand-assembly, and the higher loss tangent of the cyanoacrylate adhesive compared to the polyimide substrate.

Section 06

Array: RCS & Phase

The same characterization was repeated for the full 3×3 array. CST predicts an array resonance of −24.2 dBsm at 2.10 GHz, with a 3.3 rad phase span at that peak, but only limited phase variation across bending angles, since the simulation assumes a symmetric bending axis.

Experimentally, the array shows a broad high-RCS region from 4.09 GHz onward (around −20 dBsm). Within that region, at 5.02 GHz (RCS≈ −20.5 dBsm), the phase span is 2.38 rad; in an RCS trough at 5.43 GHz, it rises to 3.22 rad, close to CST's predicted 3.3 rad despite the resonance itself having shifted by more than 3 GHz. Phase results for both the unit cell and and array are nomarlized to a common zero reference.

Section 07

Vibration Sensing : Simulation of proof of concept

We used data from the CST model to simulate a backscattered signal under a 100 Hz periodic vibration. Its FFT shows components spaced by 100 Hz, illustrating how vibration frequency could appear in the RF return. This is a simulated demonstration; a dynamic experiment is still needed to verify vibration sensing and calibrate the response against physical vibration amplitude.

The result show an FFT of the complex scattered field σe⁻ʲᵠ revealed clear sidebands at the vibration frequency and its harmonics, confirming that the sensor encodes vibration frequency directly into the backscattered signal.

Section 08

Conclusions & Next Steps

The static CST and NRL-arch results show high RCS values in both simulation and experiment across all bending angles, with bend-dependent variations in phase for the unit cell and array. A separate CST-derived 100 Hz simulation illustrates how periodic motion could produce spectral components at the vibration frequency. Together, these findings support further testing of the proposed sensing mechanism. Dynamic measurements, repeatability analysis and environmental testing are needed before an engine application can be assessed.

The main source of disagreement between simulation and experiment traces back to the hand-assembly process. Future work aim to replace the cyanoacrylate adhesive with bondply lamination, or a directly fabricated multilayer process, to reduce dielectric loss and improve layer alignment, and explores kirigami cut patterns to set the bending axis intrinsically rather than relying on external jigs.
